title: Conditional Rendering
summary: **Conditional rendering** is how a React component decides *what* (or whether) to show based on the current data — using plain JavaScript like `if`, the ternary `? :`, and the `&&` operator inside JSX.

subtopics.title: Ternary operator
subtopics.explanation: The ternary operator cond ? <A/> : <B/> picks exactly one of two elements inline inside JSX, making it ideal for either/or UI like logged-in versus logged-out. It matters because JSX only accepts expressions, and a ternary is an expression (unlike if). Keep ternaries shallow — deeply nested ternaries become hard to read, at which point a guard clause or lookup map is clearer.

subtopics.title: Logical && short-circuit
subtopics.explanation: The expression cond && <A/> renders <A/> only when cond is truthy, and nothing when it's falsy, making it the go-to for show-or-nothing UI. It matters because it's concise, but it has a notorious gotcha: && returns its left operand when that operand is falsy, so a number like 0 gets returned and React renders a literal 0 on screen. Always coerce the left side to a real boolean.

subtopics.title: Returning null
subtopics.explanation: A component (or a branch of JSX) can return null to render nothing at all, which is cleaner than wrapping an entire tree in a condition. This matters because it lets a component opt out of rendering entirely — for example a Modal that returns null when closed. React mounts no DOM for a null branch, so it's also efficient for hiding heavy subtrees.

subtopics.title: Guard clauses
subtopics.explanation: Guard clauses use early returns at the top of a component to handle special cases — loading, error, empty — before the main happy-path JSX. This matters because it keeps the primary render flat and readable instead of buried in nested ternaries. Order matters: check loading first, then error, then empty, so you never read data that doesn't exist yet or flash an empty state during the first load.

subtopics.title: Lookup maps
subtopics.explanation: A lookup map is an object that maps each discrete case (like a status string) to the element it should render, picked with views[status]. It matters because when there are many branches, a map is far more readable and extensible than a chain of ternaries or repeated if statements — adding a case is one line. Use a ?? null fallback so an unexpected key renders nothing safely instead of undefined.
subtopics.example:
const views = { loading: <Spinner/>, error: <Err/>, success: <Data/> };
return views[status] ?? null;

subtopics.title: What React renders vs skips
subtopics.explanation: React renders strings and numbers — including 0 — as text nodes, but it ignores false, null, and undefined, rendering nothing for them. This matters because it's the root cause of the literal-0 bug: 0 is falsy in JavaScript but is still a renderable child to React. Knowing exactly which values React skips lets you reason about why a stray 0 or empty string appears and how to coerce conditions to a clean boolean.

subtopics.title: Loading / empty / error states
subtopics.explanation: Async data passes through distinct phases — loading, error, empty, and data — and a production component models each one explicitly. This matters because rendering as if data always exists causes flashes of wrong content (an 'empty' message before data arrives) and crashes when reading undefined on failure. Treat it like a small state machine and handle the phases in priority order with guard clauses.

foundations.overview: Conditional rendering means choosing what UI to produce depending on the current state or props. Because JSX is just JavaScript expressions, React has no special 'if' syntax — you use the normal language tools (if statements, the ternary operator, and &&) to decide which elements to return.
foundations.formalDefinition: Conditional rendering is the practice of returning different React elements (or nothing) from a component based on a boolean condition. Common forms are an `if` statement before the return, a ternary `cond ? <A/> : <B/>` inside JSX, the short-circuit `cond && <A/>`, and `return null` to render nothing.
foundations.whyItMatters: Real interfaces change with their data: a button is disabled until a form is valid, a spinner shows while data loads, an empty-state message appears when a list is empty. Conditional rendering is how you express all of these, so it is one of the first skills every React developer needs.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of your component as a function that is asked 'given this data, what should the screen look like right now?'. Conditional rendering is the set of if-this-then-that rules inside that function. Each render answers the question fresh from the current state.
foundations.browserPerspective: When a condition changes (because state or props changed), React re-runs the component, gets a new element tree, diffs it against the previous one, and updates only the DOM nodes that actually changed. Elements you conditionally remove are unmounted; elements you conditionally add are mounted.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Showing a spinner while fetching, an error banner on failure, an 'empty cart' message, a logged-in vs logged-out navbar, feature flags, role-based UI, and disabling submit buttons until input is valid.
foundations.businessImpact: Clear loading, empty, and error states are what make a product feel trustworthy. A blank screen during a fetch or a crash on missing data drives users away, so getting conditional UI right directly affects retention and conversion.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Most rendering bugs new developers hit — a stray literal 0 on screen, a crash on undefined data, the wrong branch showing — are conditional-rendering mistakes. Mastering the patterns removes a whole category of defects.
foundations.performanceImpact: Conditionals are cheap, but the branch you choose decides how much UI mounts. Avoid mounting heavy subtrees you immediately hide; instead render nothing (return null or skip with &&) so React does no work for the hidden branch.
commonUseCases: Showing a loading spinner, then data, then an error message
Rendering an empty-state message when a list has no items
Logged-in vs logged-out navigation and role-based UI
Toggling a modal, dropdown, or accordion open/closed

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can put an `if` statement directly inside JSX.
commonMisconceptions.reality: JSX only accepts expressions, not statements. Use a ternary or && inside JSX, or move the `if` above the return statement.

commonMisconceptions.myth: `{count && <Badge/>}` is a safe way to render the badge only when there are items.
commonMisconceptions.reality: When count is 0, `0 && <Badge/>` evaluates to 0, and React renders the literal number 0 on screen. Use `count > 0 && <Badge/>` or a ternary instead.

visualExplorer.title: How a component decides what to render
visualExplorer.caption: Walk through the decision a component makes on each render: read the data, pick a branch, return the matching UI (or nothing).

config.intro: On every render, React asks your component what to show. Conditional rendering is the set of branches that answer that question from the current state.

steps.name: Read the current state
steps.detail: The component reads its props and state — for example isLoading, error, and a list of items.

steps.name: Check the guard cases first
steps.detail: Handle the special cases up top: if isLoading, return a spinner; if error, return an error message.

steps.name: Handle the empty case
steps.detail: If the data loaded but the list is empty, return a friendly empty-state message instead of a blank screen.

steps.name: Render the happy path
steps.detail: If none of the guards matched, return the normal UI built from the data.

steps.name: Or render nothing
steps.detail: When there is genuinely nothing to show, return null so React mounts no DOM for that branch.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A heading that switches between 'Welcome back!' and 'Please log in.' as you click the button.

codeLab.title: Show an empty-state message
codeLab.instructions: Given a `cart` array in state, render a list of items when there are any, and the message 'Your cart is empty' when there are none. Use a ternary or guard clause — not `cart && ...`.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Empty cart shows 'Your cart is empty'; after clicking Add, the items appear in a list.
hints: Use cart.length === 0 to detect the empty case explicitly.
A ternary lets you return one of two elements: cart.length === 0 ? <empty/> : <list/>.

debuggingLab.title: The mysterious literal 0 on screen
debuggingLab.symptom: When the cart is empty, the page shows a stray '0' instead of nothing. The badge appears correctly only after items are added.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The expression `count && <span/>` short-circuits: when count is 0, JavaScript evaluates `0 && anything` to `0`. React renders the numbers it is given, and 0 is a valid React child, so a literal 0 appears on screen. (false, null, and undefined render nothing — but 0 is not falsy in that special sense to React; it is a renderable number.)
commonMistakes: Using a number directly as the left side of && (`count && ...`) instead of a real boolean.
Assuming React skips rendering all falsy values — it skips false/null/undefined, but renders 0 and empty strings.
Forgetting that empty strings ('') also render as nothing-visible but are still a child.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Change the condition so the badge shows only when count is greater than 0 and nothing renders when it is 0. Convert the left side of && into a real boolean.

theory.question: What are the main ways to do conditional rendering in React?
theory.directAnswer: Because JSX is JavaScript, you use normal language constructs: an `if` statement before the return, the ternary operator `cond ? <A/> : <B/>` inside JSX, the logical `&&` for show-or-nothing, and `return null` to render nothing at all. You can also use a lookup object/map to pick among many branches.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Choosing which React elements (or none) a component returns based on a condition.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: UIs must reflect changing data — loading vs loaded, empty vs full, authorized vs not — so components need a way to branch.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: JSX expressions accept other expressions, so a ternary or && evaluates to an element or to a non-rendered value (false/null/undefined). Statements like `if` go outside JSX, typically computing a variable that you then render.

theory.whyImportant: Conditional rendering appears in almost every component, and the patterns (plus the &&/0 pitfall) are extremely common beginner interview questions.
theory.realWorldExample: A data table shows a spinner while loading, an error banner on failure, an empty-state when there are no rows, and the table when data arrives.

nestedTopics.title: Ternary operator
nestedTopics.explanation: `cond ? <A/> : <B/>` picks exactly one of two elements inline; ideal for either/or UI.

nestedTopics.title: Logical && short-circuit
nestedTopics.explanation: `cond && <A/>` renders <A/> when cond is truthy and nothing when it is falsy — but beware numbers like 0.

nestedTopics.title: Returning null
nestedTopics.explanation: A component can `return null` to render nothing, which is cleaner than wrapping the whole tree in a condition.

followUps.question: Why can't you use an `if` statement directly inside JSX?
followUps.answer: JSX curly braces accept expressions, and `if` is a statement, not an expression. Use a ternary/&& inside JSX, or move the `if` above the return.

followUps.question: When would you prefer a lookup map over a chain of ternaries?
followUps.answer: When there are many discrete cases (e.g., status -> component). A map like `views[status]` is more readable and extensible than nested `? :`.

theory.question: Why does `{count && <Badge/>}` sometimes render a literal 0, and how do you avoid it?
theory.directAnswer: When count is 0, `0 && <Badge/>` short-circuits to 0, and React renders the number 0 as a text node. Avoid it by making the left side a real boolean: `count > 0 && <Badge/>`, or use a ternary `count > 0 ? <Badge/> : null`.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A rendering bug caused by using a number as the left operand of the && operator inside JSX.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: `&&` returns its left operand when that operand is falsy. 0 is falsy in JavaScript, so the whole expression becomes 0 — and React treats 0 as a renderable child (unlike false/null/undefined, which render nothing).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Converting the condition to a boolean (`count > 0`, or `Boolean(count)`, or `!!count`) makes && return either true-ish element or `false`, which React skips.

theory.whyImportant: This is one of the most common React bugs and a favorite interview gotcha because it reveals whether a candidate understands both JS truthiness and how React renders values.
theory.realWorldExample: A notifications badge `{unread && <Badge>{unread}</Badge>}` shows a stray 0 when there are no unread messages.

nestedTopics.title: What React renders vs skips
nestedTopics.explanation: React renders strings and numbers (including 0); it ignores false, null, undefined, and true.

nestedTopics.title: Coercing to boolean
nestedTopics.explanation: Use comparisons (count > 0), Boolean(x), or !!x to ensure && never returns a renderable number.

nestedTopics.title: Ternary as the safe alternative
nestedTopics.explanation: `cond ? <A/> : null` never accidentally renders the condition value itself.

followUps.question: Does the same problem happen with empty strings?
followUps.answer: Yes — `'' && <A/>` returns '', which renders as an (invisible) empty text node. The fix is the same: use an explicit boolean.

followUps.question: Is `!!count && <Badge/>` acceptable?
followUps.answer: It works, but `count > 0` is usually clearer about intent. Use whichever your team finds more readable.

scenario.question: A component that fetches users sometimes flashes 'No users found' before the data appears, and crashes when the request fails. How do you structure the rendering?
scenario.directAnswer: Model the UI as distinct states — loading, error, empty, and data — and handle them with explicit guard clauses in priority order. Check loading first, then error, then empty, then render the data. This prevents the empty-state flash (it only shows after loading finishes) and avoids reading data that doesn't exist on error.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A state-machine approach to conditional rendering that covers every phase of an async operation.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Async data passes through several phases; rendering as if data always exists leads to flashes of wrong content and crashes on undefined.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Use early returns or a computed `content` variable: `if (loading) ...; if (error) ...; if (items.length === 0) ...; else render list`. Order matters — empty must be checked only after loading is false.

scenario.whyImportant: Handling all four states cleanly is a hallmark of production-ready components and a frequent practical interview discussion.

nestedTopics.title: Guard clauses / early returns
nestedTopics.explanation: Return the special-case UI first so the happy-path JSX stays flat and readable.

nestedTopics.title: State priority order
nestedTopics.explanation: Loading and error take precedence over empty/data to avoid flashes and undefined reads.

followUps.question: How do you prevent the empty-state from flashing during the first load?
followUps.answer: Only evaluate the empty condition when loading is false; while loading is true, the loading branch wins.

coding.question: Build a component that takes a `status` ('loading' | 'success' | 'error') and renders the right message using a lookup map instead of nested ternaries.
coding.thoughtProcess: With several discrete cases, a lookup object keyed by status is cleaner than chained ternaries. I map each status to an element and render `views[status]`, falling back to null for unknown values so it never crashes.
coding.lineByLine: The `views` object maps each status string to a React element. `views[status]` looks up the element for the current status. The `?? null` fallback guarantees nothing renders (instead of `undefined` causing issues) when the key is missing. Buttons change status to demonstrate each branch.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — a fixed-size map of elements.

alternativeApproaches.title: Nested ternaries
alternativeApproaches.explanation: `status === 'loading' ? ... : status === 'error' ? ... : ...` works but quickly becomes hard to read as cases grow.

alternativeApproaches.title: switch statement before return
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A switch computing a `content` variable is also clear and lets each branch run extra logic.

followUps.question: Why use `?? null` rather than just `views[status]`?
followUps.answer: If status is ever an unexpected value, the lookup is undefined; `?? null` makes the intent explicit and renders nothing safely.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Model UI as explicit states (loading/error/empty/data) and render with guard clauses or a lookup map. Keep the branching logic in the component that owns the data, and extract a small presentational component per state if a branch grows complex.
productionDeepDive.performance: Conditionals themselves are negligible, but the branch you pick decides how much mounts. Render null for hidden branches rather than mounting and hiding with CSS when the subtree is heavy. Avoid recreating large element objects on every render inside conditions.
productionDeepDive.security: When rendering role-based UI, treat client-side conditionals as cosmetic only — never rely on hiding a button to enforce authorization. The server must still reject unauthorized actions regardless of what the UI shows.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As the number of states grows, replace long ternary chains with a lookup map or a small state machine so adding a case is one line rather than restructuring nested expressions.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Prefer early-return guard clauses for the happy path to stay flat. Convert numbers to booleans before && to avoid the literal-0 bug. Name branches clearly (isLoading, hasError, isEmpty).
productionDeepDive.observability: Wrong-branch bugs are best caught by rendering the state name in development overlays and by React DevTools, where you can inspect props/state to see why a particular branch was chosen.

caseStudies.problem: A notifications badge showed a stray '0' for users with no unread items.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: None meaningful — just a more correct boolean condition.
caseStudies.lessons: Always coerce numeric conditions to booleans before using && in JSX.

keyTakeaways: JSX has no special if-syntax — use the ternary, &&, an if before the return, or a lookup map.
`{count && <X/>}` renders a literal 0 when count is 0; coerce to a boolean with `count > 0`.
React renders strings and numbers (including 0) but ignores false, null, and undefined.
Model async UI as loading/error/empty/data and handle them with guard clauses in priority order.
Client-side conditional UI is cosmetic — never rely on it to enforce authorization.
